reason: The passage establishes this principle through narrative contrast: God demonstrates good leadership by hearing the Israelites' cries ('וַיִּשְׁמַע אֱלֹהִים אֶת־ נַאֲקָתָם'), remembering covenant obligations ('וַיִּזְכֹּר אֱלֹהִים אֶת־ בְּרִיתוֹ'), and responding with action to free them ('וְהוֹצֵאתִי אֶתְכֶ֖ם'). This compassionate response stands in direct contrast to Pharaoh's leadership model—he hardens his heart ('וַיֶּחֱזַק לֵב־ פַּרְעֹה') and refuses to listen to the pleas of his enslaved people. While not explicitly didactic, the passage implicitly models compassion and responsiveness to human suffering as the basis of righteous leadership, demonstrated through God's actions and contrasted with Pharaoh's cruelty.
